title: When should you use Select projection instead of Include?
description: DTO projections that fetch only what you need, cartesian explosion, and when full entities are actually right.

data.text: **Question:** When should you use Select projection instead of Include?

`Include` loads **entire entities** and their graphs — convenient when you intend to track and modify them. `Select` projection materializes only the columns your DTO needs — smaller payloads, no change tracking, often fewer joins. Prefer projection for **read-only** endpoints (lists, reports, API responses); prefer `Include` when the entities will be **modified and saved** through the same DbContext. Combining many `Include`s of collections causes **cartesian explosion** — split queries or project instead.

**Include:**
- `Include(b => b.Posts).ThenInclude(p => p.Comments)` — one entity graph, tracked by default
- Required for EF to know the graph when you save navigation changes (adding a child to a loaded collection)
- Every included collection multiplies rows in a single JOIN — three 100-row collections → 1,000,000 combined rows before EF dedupes client-side (**cartesian explosion**); `AsSplitQuery()` issues one query per root+collection instead, trading joins for round-trips
- Full entities carry every column (including heavy ones you don't display) and pay tracking overhead

**Projection:**
- `.Select(b => new BlogCardDto(b.Id, b.Url, b.Posts.Count))` — SQL fetches exactly these columns/aggregates
- Results are **not tracked** — reads are cheaper and the context stays lean (you can't accidentally SaveChanges a DTO)
- Collections of primitives/DTOs are supported (`Select(b => new BlogDto { Tags = b.Posts.Select(...) })`) — no navigation graph at all
- Aggregates, counts, and computed values happen **in SQL** instead of loading rows to count in memory
- Can even project to types EF never mapped (`Select(p => new { p.Title, Recent = ... })`, tuples, existing DTOs)

**Rule of thumb:**
- Endpoint only displays data → projection (or `AsNoTracking` + Include when you truly need graph shape)
- Endpoint edits and saves the same aggregate → `Include` (tracking is the point)
- Report/analytics → projection with `AsNoTracking` even if 'graph-shaped'
- Sorting/filtering on large sets → do it in SQL before projection; never filter client-side after loading

data.title: Graph load vs tight projection

data.text:
Interviewers want to assess:
- Knowing projection returns untracked DTOs and smaller SQL
- Understanding cartesian explosion and the AsSplitQuery fix
- The edit-vs-read distinction: Include exists for tracked graph mutations
- Doing counts/filters/aggregates in SQL, not in memory

items: Including five collections in one query — exponential row growth and huge memory spikes
Projecting, then expecting SaveChanges to persist navigation changes (results aren't tracked)
Loading full entities to compute counts/sums in memory
Client-side evaluation after ToList: filtering/sorting in C# because 'the LINQ was complex'
Selecting all columns (`Select(x => x)`) — that's just a more expensive Include
Forgetting indexes on columns used in the WHERE/ORDER BY of projections — the SQL still has to find rows
How do you page a list efficiently while filtering on a related collection?
When would you choose AsNoTracking with Include over projection?
How do you project into an existing DTO that lives in another project?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Include = tracked full graph; Select = lean, untracked, SQL-shaped output
Many collection Includes → cartesian explosion → AsSplitQuery or project
Counts, filters, and sorting belong in SQL before materialization
Projection for reads; Include when the same graph will be saved
data.takeaway: Fetch exactly what the screen needs — projection by default, Include only when tracking a graph you're about to modify.
